```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This is a worked test of `taxonAlign` against real, messy data, not a hand-built example. The dataset
is `Prendergast_2026_3` (from the sibling `austraits.build` repository) -- a plant-pollinator
visitation dataset recording which animals were observed visiting which plant species: bees, wasps,
flies, beetles and butterflies, but also birds, bats, a possum and a skink. Animal identifications in
a dataset like this are exactly the kind of thing `taxonAlign` is built to clean up: misspellings
(`"Hymnoptera"`, `"Psittaformes"`), morphospecies codes, bracketed subgenera
(`"Amegilla (Zonamegilla) aeruginosa"`), outdated names, and more.

We align the raw animal names, at both species level (`Animal species binomial name`) and order level
(`Animal order`), against two of the reference lists in taxonAlign's first data release, and look at
what kinds of matches get made in each case: first the
[Australian Faunal Directory](https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/home) (AFD, in its National Species List
format), then GBIF's list of Australian animals.

```{r setup}
library(taxonAlign)
library(dplyr)
```

## Building the AFD reference

```{r}
afd <- load_taxonomic_resources("NSL_animals", version = "2026-10-07", quiet = TRUE)
afd_resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(afd)
```

`prepare_taxonomic_resources()` drops a handful of real AFD records here (with a warning, hidden in
this document): placeholder names such as `"Genus A"`, recorded for undescribed taxa, which could
never be usefully matched against and would only attract false fuzzy matches.

## Loading the data to align

```{r}
pollinator_data <- readr::read_csv(
  "../../austraits.build/data/Prendergast_2026_3/data.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

pollinator_data |>
  select(`Animal species binomial name`, `Animal order`) |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

`r nrow(pollinator_data)` rows in total, spanning `r n_distinct(pollinator_data[["Animal species binomial name"]])`
distinct animal names and `r n_distinct(pollinator_data[["Animal order"]])` distinct orders.

## A helper to align a column and summarise the results

The same name is often repeated across many observations, so each *distinct* name is aligned once
(much faster than aligning all `r format(nrow(pollinator_data), big.mark = ",")` rows directly) and the result is joined back onto every
observation that used it -- every count below is therefore at the observation level, not just the
distinct-name level.

```{r}
align_column <- function(x, resources) {
  distinct_names <- sort(unique(x))
  aligned <- align_taxa(distinct_names, resources)
  tibble(original_name = x) |>
    left_join(aligned, by = "original_name")
}

# a short, human-readable label for each match, derived directly from columns align_taxa() already
# returns (chars_changed == 0 means an exact match; taxonomic_status is the *matched* row's own
# status) -- not a hand-maintained lookup of every internal alignment_code
summarise_match_types <- function(aligned) {
  aligned |>
    mutate(
      match_type = case_when(
        is.na(alignment_code) ~ "No match",
        chars_changed == 0 ~ paste0("Exact match — ", taxon_rank, " (", taxonomic_status, ")"),
        TRUE ~ paste0("Fuzzy match — ", taxon_rank, " (", taxonomic_status, ")")
      )
    ) |>
    count(match_type, sort = TRUE, name = "n_observations")
}

# the full internal breakdown -- one row per distinct match block/pattern that actually fired
detailed_match_breakdown <- function(aligned) {
  aligned |>
    mutate(alignment_code = coalesce(alignment_code, "(no match)")) |>
    count(alignment_code, sort = TRUE, name = "n_observations")
}

match_examples <- function(aligned, detailed_counts, n_examples = 5) {
  aligned |>
    mutate(alignment_code = coalesce(alignment_code, "(no match)")) |>
    distinct(alignment_code, original_name, aligned_name, taxon_rank) |>
    group_by(alignment_code) |>
    slice_head(n = n_examples) |>
    ungroup() |>
    left_join(detailed_counts, by = "alignment_code") |>
    arrange(alignment_code, original_name) |>
    select(alignment_code, n_observations, original_name, aligned_name, taxon_rank)
}

# every distinct name that got no match at all, with how many observations it accounts for -- lets a
# reviewer prioritise which gaps are worth fixing first, without scrolling past the same repeated name
# dozens of times
unmatched_names <- function(aligned) {
  aligned |>
    filter(is.na(aligned_name)) |>
    count(original_name, sort = TRUE, name = "n_observations")
}
```

## Aligning by species binomial name

```{r}
species_aligned <- align_column(pollinator_data[["Animal species binomial name"]], afd_resources)
```

### Counts of each match type

```{r}
summarise_match_types(species_aligned) |> knitr::kable()
```

### Detailed breakdown (internal match code)

Each code names the specific string pattern/rule that matched -- e.g. `match_01c_accepted_canonical_name`
is an exact match to an accepted species' canonical name, `match_02c_fuzzy_genus_accepted` is a fuzzy
match to a genus, and so on.

```{r}
species_detail <- detailed_match_breakdown(species_aligned)
species_detail |> knitr::kable()
```

### Examples of each

```{r}
match_examples(species_aligned, species_detail) |> knitr::kable()
```

### All non-matched names

Every distinct name that got no match at all, together with how many observations it accounts for --
`r sum(is.na(species_aligned$aligned_name))` observations in total, covering
`r n_distinct(species_aligned$original_name[is.na(species_aligned$aligned_name)])` distinct names.
This is the working list for deciding what actually needs fixing (a typo to correct, a name to add to
the reference, a non-taxonomic entry to filter out before aligning, ...).

```{r}
species_unmatched <- unmatched_names(species_aligned)
species_unmatched |> knitr::kable()
```

## Aligning by order

```{r}
order_aligned <- align_column(pollinator_data[["Animal order"]], afd_resources)
```

### Counts of each match type

```{r}
summarise_match_types(order_aligned) |> knitr::kable()
```

### Detailed breakdown (internal match code)

```{r}
order_detail <- detailed_match_breakdown(order_aligned)
order_detail |> knitr::kable()
```

### Examples of each

```{r}
match_examples(order_aligned, order_detail) |> knitr::kable()
```

## The vertebrate visitors

The AFD covers Australian animals of every kind, vertebrates included, so the birds, bats, possum
and skink in this dataset are matched the same way as the insects -- including their orders, and the
misspelt `"Psittaformes"`, which fuzzy-matches `"Psittaciformes"`. Their species names show
`update_taxa()` at work: honeyeaters recorded under the old genus *Lichenostomus*, which has since been
split, are updated to their current genera (*Gavicalis*, *Caligavis*, *Ptilotula*, *Nesoptilotis*), and
misspellings (`"Melithrepotus brevirostris"`, `"Rhipidura fulginosa"`) are corrected.

```{r}
vertebrates <- pollinator_data |> filter(`Animal class` %in% c("Aves", "Mammalia", "Reptilia"))
vertebrate_names <- sort(unique(vertebrates[["Animal species binomial name"]]))

afd_vertebrates <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(vertebrate_names, afd_resources)
afd_vertebrates |>
  select(original_name, suggested_name, taxon_rank, taxonomic_status_aligned) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

A few names only reach genus. Three are old combinations the AFD doesn't list under that name:
*Phylidonyris albifrons* (now *Purnella albifrons*), *Anthochaera rufogularis* (now *Acanthagenys
rufogularis*) and *Climacteris leucophaca*, a misspelling of *Climacteris leucophaea* (now *Cormobates
leucophaea*; the AFD lists only its old subspecies names under *Climacteris*). The next section tries
GBIF's list for these.

## Comparing with GBIF's list of Australian animals

The data release also has `"GBIF_AU"`: every animal in the GBIF backbone taxonomy with occurrence
records in Australia, plus its synonyms. GBIF's occurrence records include fossil specimens, so taxa
GBIF flags as extinct are left out by default.

```{r}
gbif <- load_taxonomic_resources("GBIF_AU", version = "2026-10-07", quiet = TRUE)
gbif_resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(gbif)
```

`r format(nrow(gbif$GBIF_AU), big.mark = ",")` records -- about
`r round(nrow(gbif$GBIF_AU) / nrow(afd$NSL_animals), 1)`x the size of the AFD list above.

### Aligning by species binomial name

```{r}
gbif_species_aligned <- align_column(pollinator_data[["Animal species binomial name"]], gbif_resources)
```

#### Counts of each match type

```{r}
summarise_match_types(gbif_species_aligned) |> knitr::kable()
```

#### Detailed breakdown (internal match code)

```{r}
gbif_species_detail <- detailed_match_breakdown(gbif_species_aligned)
gbif_species_detail |> knitr::kable()
```

#### Examples of each

```{r}
match_examples(gbif_species_aligned, gbif_species_detail) |> knitr::kable()
```

#### All non-matched names

```{r}
unmatched_names(gbif_species_aligned) |> knitr::kable()
```

### Aligning by order

```{r}
gbif_order_aligned <- align_column(pollinator_data[["Animal order"]], gbif_resources)
```

#### Counts of each match type

```{r}
summarise_match_types(gbif_order_aligned) |> knitr::kable()
```

#### Detailed breakdown (internal match code)

```{r}
gbif_order_detail <- detailed_match_breakdown(gbif_order_aligned)
gbif_order_detail |> knitr::kable()
```

#### Examples of each

```{r}
match_examples(gbif_order_aligned, gbif_order_detail) |> knitr::kable()
```

### The vertebrates, by each reference, and both combined

In practice you'd use the two together, listing the AFD first: where both have an accepted name, the
AFD's is the one matched, and GBIF adds the names the AFD lacks. (Where both list the same *old* name,
the record with the higher-priority taxonomic status is matched, whichever reference it's in -- GBIF's
plain "synonym" record for *Lichenostomus leucotis* is matched before the AFD's "Generic combination"
one, though both lead to *Nesoptilotis leucotis*.)

```{r}
both_resources <- prepare_taxonomic_resources(c(afd, gbif))

gbif_vertebrates <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(vertebrate_names, gbif_resources)
both_vertebrates <- create_taxonomic_update_lookup(vertebrate_names, both_resources)

# compared without the subgenus, which the AFD writes into a species' name where it has one
# ("Acanthiza (Geobasileus) chrysorrhoa") and GBIF doesn't
without_subgenus <- function(x) coalesce(sub(" \\([^)]*\\)", "", x), "(no match)")

tibble(
  original_name = vertebrate_names,
  AFD = afd_vertebrates$suggested_name,
  GBIF = gbif_vertebrates$suggested_name,
  `AFD, then GBIF` = both_vertebrates$suggested_name
) |>
  filter(without_subgenus(AFD) != without_subgenus(GBIF) | without_subgenus(AFD) != original_name) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Only the names whose suggested name differs from the name recorded, or between the two references,
are listed.

## Summary

Aligning `Animal species binomial name` against the AFD resolved
`r sum(!is.na(species_aligned$aligned_name))` of `r nrow(species_aligned)` observations
(`r round(100 * mean(!is.na(species_aligned$aligned_name)), 1)`%), and against GBIF's Australian
animals, `r sum(!is.na(gbif_species_aligned$aligned_name))`
(`r round(100 * mean(!is.na(gbif_species_aligned$aligned_name)), 1)`%). Aligning `Animal order`
resolved `r sum(!is.na(order_aligned$aligned_name))` of `r nrow(order_aligned)` observations against
the AFD (`r round(100 * mean(!is.na(order_aligned$aligned_name)), 1)`%) and
`r sum(!is.na(gbif_order_aligned$aligned_name))`
(`r round(100 * mean(!is.na(gbif_order_aligned$aligned_name)), 1)`%) against GBIF. Resolving a name
isn't the same as resolving it well, though: the examples above show where each reference only got as
far as a genus, and where a fuzzy match is worth a second look. Across all four alignments, this single
real dataset exercised
`r length(unique(c(species_aligned$alignment_code, order_aligned$alignment_code, gbif_species_aligned$alignment_code, gbif_order_aligned$alignment_code)))`
distinct internal match patterns -- a reasonable stand-in for how varied real-world taxonomic name
data actually is.
